rationale: A wins because it knows where the facts stop. Its best line, "The store that costs more to build is the one Warby says pays off," turns the update into a real investor question while explicitly refusing to invent exam revenue. B has usable material, but "Warby Parker was supposed to make optical stores obsolete" is a magazine-y premise the supplied facts do not prove, and "a large new employer of optometrists" gets ahead of the staffing model before the basics are known.
gaps_in_A: "a brand that started as a glasses-by-mail disruptor" and "A DTC eyewear brand" lean on Warby background not supplied in the update. The angle still works, but the fact trail is not as clean as it pretends.

"the historically defensible, insurance-tied part of the optical business the incumbents have owned" is plausible industry framing, not a provided fact. It needs sourcing before it goes near a reporter.
The retail-health trend angle admits its own weakness: "without it, this is a one-company observation, not yet a trend." Correctly flagged, but still a ceiling on news value.
The pharmacy angle is honest but thin: "an unnamed-partner pilot has almost no reportable detail yet." It belongs in the maybe pile until the chain and scope are confirmed.
gaps_in_B: "Warby Parker was supposed to make optical stores obsolete" is too confident for the provided facts. The update mentions online-only customers; it does not prove a founding premise or a failed anti-store ideology.

"Warby Parker's retail expansion means a large new employer of optometrists" overstates the evidence. "Most" of 40 stores could be meaningful, but "large new employer" assumes hiring volume and employment model the set later admits it does not know.
"profitability enables expansion" smuggles in a capital-allocation claim. The facts say Warby recently reached profitability and is opening stores; they do not say profits fund the expansion.
Angle 1 and Angle 4 crowd the same exam-staffing fact. Retail-health strategy and optometrist workforce are different desks, but without hard staffing numbers the second one looks like padding.
